newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Bhutto accuses Islamists of plotting her downfall.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto accuses Islamists of plotting her downfall.

text.p: Pakistan's ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto accused shadowy Islamist forces on Thursday of plotting her downfall, but absolved the military of all blame.

She said Moslem extremists had been conspiring to overthrow democracy ever since her father Zulfikar Ali Bhutto founded the Pakistan People's Party (PPP) in 1967. He was toppled by General Mohammed Zia-ul-Haq in 1977 and hanged two years later.
"There are anti-Bhutto, anti-PPP forces and ex-Zia forces...who want to bring a soft Islamic revolution," Bhutto said in an interview with Reuters television.
"They want to get rid of me because they think that I'm a modern leader and they don't want to see a liberal Pakistan."
Bhutto, unceremoniously sacked by President Farooq Leghari in the early hours on Tuesday, vowed to fight back, but said elections could only be fair if Leghari stepped down.
The president nominated a caretaker prime minister, Meraj Khalid, to run the country until polls set for February 3.
Bhutto, 43, said she had no faith in the neutrality of Leghari, once a close political associate, saying he had acted in a "shabby" manner to grasp power for himself.

"Because I want a fair election, I'm demanding that the president step down and that there should be a neutral caretaker government," she said. "If the elections are not perceived to be fair, there's going to be an agitation."
Leghari cited corruption, nepotism and misrule among a long list of reasons for his decision to remove Bhutto's three-year government and dissolve the National Assembly (lower house).

Political observers said he could not have acted without the tacit support of the army, but Bhutto disputed that view, saying troops who moved into Islamabad soon after her dismissal were only following the orders of the president.

"Let me tell you that the army was not involved," she said. "The armed forces, the present chief of army staff, stayed out of it. He was neutral. He was probably aware of what was going on, but he wasn't going to be intrusive."
Bhutto was speaking at the prime minister's official residence, where she was held for about 36 hours after her dismissal before curbs on her movements were lifted.
She said she planned to leave her opulent official mansion within the next few days for accommodation in Islamabad.
Her three children ran down a corridor to greet her, while her own mother Nusrat paced more slowly, still in mourning for her son Murtaza, killed by Karachi police on September 20.
Bhutto said she believed that her detained husband, Asif Ali Zardari, would face fabricated charges in connection with the killing of her estranged brother.

"I think they are holding him because they are trying to persuade my sister-in-law (Murtaza's widow Ghinwa) to file a case against him," she declared. "I hope she doesn't fall prey to this, but then anything can happen because reality is stranger than fiction."

Zardari, investment minister in Bhutto's cabinet, was detained without charge on Tuesday in Lahore and transferred to an official resthouse near Islamabad, where Bhutto was allowed to visit him in the early hours of Thursday.
She said he was being held by the military's Inter-Services Intelligence, but had been placed in police custody on Thursday under an order citing the maintenance of peace.
Zardari is at the centre of corruption allegations swirling around Bhutto's former government, but she said he had done nothing wrong. "So where are these charges?" she demanded.
